passage:
"Didi, the new man at Kaka's house doesn't talk to anyone," Vijay said, peeling a groundnut. "He sits on the step and reads books all evening."
"So?" Sarita asked, not looking up from her homework.
"So he's a librarian. Obviously."
"Why obviously?"
"Quiet. Books. Glasses. That's a librarian."
"Vijay, how many libraries are there in our whole taluka?"
He thought. "One. Near the bus stand."
"And how many farms?"
"Hundreds. Everyone has a farm."
"So which is there more of, librarians or farmers?"
Vijay frowned at the groundnut shell. "Farmers... but he really looks like a librarian!"
"Farmers can like books too. Appa reads the newspaper twice every morning."
"Hmm. Maybe he's a farmer who reads," Vijay said slowly. "I'm still asking him tomorrow."

qa.q: What does the new man at Kaka's house do every evening?
qa.a: He sits on the step and reads books all evening.

qa.q: Why does it feel so obvious to Vijay that the man is a librarian?
qa.a: Vijay feels confident because the man is quiet, with books and glasses, matching Vijay's picture of a librarian so well that the match feels like proof. Vijay forgets there is one library but hundreds of farms.

qa.q: What question helped Vijay, and what could he ask himself next time?
qa.a: Sarita's question about how many libraries and farms made him count. Next time he could first ask how many people around him do each job, and only then look at the clues.

qa.q: How might the new man feel if Vijay told him, "You must be the librarian"?
qa.a: He might be amused or puzzled, especially if he is a farmer who simply enjoys reading in the evening.

grounding: It shows a child jumping from 'quiet and reads books' to 'librarian' while forgetting how many more farmers there are.

passage: My name is Disha, and last summer I made a silly guess. Mehak's uncle came to stay with them in our building. He hardly spoke at dinner, and he carried a thick book everywhere, even into the lift. I whispered to Mehak, "Your uncle is a librarian, right?" She laughed so hard. "He grows sugarcane in Mandya!" My face went hot. Later Mehak's mother said something I still think about. In their district there are thousands of farmers and only a few librarians. So even a quiet man with a book is much more likely to be a farmer. I only saw the book. I never thought about how many farmers there are.

qa.q: What does Mehak's uncle actually do?
qa.a: He grows sugarcane in Mandya.

qa.q: Why did the librarian guess feel right to Disha at the time?
qa.a: Disha felt confident because the uncle's quietness and his thick book matched Disha's picture of a librarian so closely that the picture felt like proof. Disha never stopped to think how few librarians there are.

qa.q: What could Disha do before making a guess like that next time?
qa.a: Disha could first think about how common each job is, like farmers compared with librarians, and then look at the clues.

qa.q: How might Mehak's uncle see it if he heard the guess?
qa.a: He might find it funny, or feel a little misread, since loving books is part of his life as a farmer too. 🙂

grounding: It shows a child guessing a job from one vivid trait while ignoring how many more farmers there are than librarians.

passage:
Class 4B, Thursday. In our guessing game today I described a stranger: a quiet man who loves reading, always with a book in his bag. Vikas shouted "Librarian!" at once, and most hands went up with him. Deepak said "farmer", mostly as a joke. I asked Vikas how many librarians he knew. "One, at the town library." How many farmers? He started counting uncles and neighbours and gave up at twenty. He looked at his fingers for a while and said, "So even if not many farmers read, there are so many of them." I did not give the answer; he got there himself. Next week I will repeat the game and write the counts on the board first.
Class teacher, 4B

qa.q: What did Vikas shout when the teacher described the quiet man who loves reading?
qa.a: "Librarian!"

qa.q: Why did 'librarian' feel like the right answer to Vikas?
qa.a: A quiet man who loves reading fits the picture of a librarian so neatly that the fit felt like proof, and Vikas did not think about how many more farmers there are.

qa.q: What is the teacher's plan for next week, and why might it help?
qa.a: Writing the counts on the board first makes the children start from how common each job is before they look at the description.

qa.q: How might Deepak have felt when his joke answer turned out to be the more sensible guess?
qa.a: Deepak might feel surprised and a bit pleased, since the answer was given only as a joke.

grounding: It shows a child choosing 'librarian' from a description while overlooking how many more farmers there are.

passage:
Tuesday, at Nani's village
This morning I went with Sangeeta to the dairy centre. A new man was standing in the milk queue with two steel cans, reading a fat book with tiny print. He didn't talk to anybody. He wore glasses.
I whispered, "He's a librarian. A hundred percent."
Sangeeta said, "He's standing in the milk queue, Lakshmi. Everyone here is a farmer. There are about three hundred farmers in this village and one library, and Nirmala aunty runs it."
But he looked EXACTLY like a librarian! Farmers don't read books like that in a queue. I bet Sangeeta my hair clips.
Nani says he took the old mango orchard near the canal. I don't care. I still think he's a librarian on holiday.
Lakshmi

qa.q: What was the new man holding in the milk queue?
qa.a: He had two steel cans and was reading a fat book with tiny print.

qa.q: Why does Lakshmi feel so sure the man is a librarian?
qa.a: The quiet man with glasses and a thick book matches Lakshmi's picture of a librarian so well that the story feels stronger than Sangeeta's numbers about three hundred farmers and one library.

qa.q: What small step could help Lakshmi test that guess before betting?
qa.a: Lakshmi could count first: in a village with about three hundred farmers and one library, a reading man in a milk queue is far more likely to be a farmer who loves books.

qa.q: How does Sangeeta see the man in the milk queue?
qa.a: Sangeeta sees what fits the village: a man with milk cans in a dairy queue where almost everyone is a farmer, so the book doesn't change much for Sangeeta.

grounding: It shows a child deciding a quiet, bookish man must be a librarian while ignoring how many more farmers there are in the village.

passage:
The tractor trolley bumped along the road to the Hosur fair, and Sangeeta, nine, and Gopika were playing Guess the Job. Across from them sat a thin man with a cloth bag full of books, turning pages and saying nothing.
"Easy," Sangeeta whispered. "He's a librarian. Or a professor."
Gopika's Appa laughed from the driver's seat. "Sangeeta, in this whole taluk, how many librarians do you know?"
She thought. "One. The lady at the reading room."
"And how many farmers?"
"Too many to count."
"So who is more likely sitting in my trolley?"
Sangeeta looked at the man again, his careful glasses, his quiet page-turning. "But he reads so much, Appa. Farmers don't carry books."
The man got down at the seed shop.

qa.q: Where was the tractor trolley going?
qa.a: It was going to the Hosur fair.

qa.q: How does Sangeeta feel about her guess, even after counting?
qa.a: Sangeeta still feels confident the man is a librarian, because his glasses and quiet page-turning fit that picture so well, even though she knows only one librarian and too many farmers to count.

qa.q: What could Sangeeta do the next time she plays Guess the Job?
qa.a: Before looking at clues, Sangeeta could first ask which jobs are most common around her, then see whether the clues are strong enough to change that guess.

qa.q: How might Gopika's Appa see the man getting down at the seed shop?
qa.a: Appa might smile, since a stop at the seed shop fits a farmer who likes reading, just as the counting suggested.

grounding: It shows a child sure a quiet reader must be a librarian, forgetting how many more farmers there are, because the story outweighs the numbers.
